questions.question: I sorted my shapes into two groups: circle, square, and triangle in Group 1; ball, cube, and can in Group 2. What is my sorting rule?
options: Group 1 has more sides. Group 2 has fewer sides.
Group 1 is the flat shapes only.
Group 1 has corners. Group 2 has no corners.
questions.explain: The circle, square, and triangle are all flat (2D) shapes. The ball, cube, and can are all 3D objects. The rule is flat vs 3D, not corners, because the circle has no corners.

questions.question: Sam sorted his toys into two groups: block, box, and can in Group 1; flat picture, paper square, and card in Group 2. What is Sam's rule?
options: Group 1 is heavy. Group 2 is light.
Group 1 takes up space. Group 2 is flat.
Group 1 has 6 sides. Group 2 has 4 sides.
questions.explain: A block, box, and can all take up space (3D). A picture, square, and card are flat (2D). The rule is 3D vs flat, not weight or number of sides.

questions.question: I put 4 shapes into two groups: triangle and square in Group 1; circle and oval in Group 2. What is my rule?
options: Group 1 is big and Group 2 is small.
Group 1 is the group with the corners.
Group 1 has corners. Group 2 does not.
Group 1 has 3 sides. Group 2 has 4 sides.
questions.explain: Triangles and squares have corners. Circles and ovals do not. The rule must tell about BOTH groups. Size does not separate these groups.

questions.question: Jade is making a shape poster. She puts the square, triangle, and rectangle on the left side. She puts the circle and oval on the right side. What rule should she write?
options: Left: big shapes. Right: small shapes.
Left: the ones that have corners.
Left: has corners. Right: no corners.
questions.explain: Squares, triangles, and rectangles all have corners. Circles and ovals do not. The rule must cover both sides. The number of sides does not match, since a square has 4 and a triangle has 3.

questions.question: Kai sorts his blocks into two piles: cube, ball, and cone in Pile 1; flat square, flat triangle, and flat circle in Pile 2. Kai says: 'Pile 1 is 3D. Pile 2 is flat.' Is this a correct rule?
options: No, it only names one pile.
questions.explain: Kai's rule works because every block in Pile 1 is 3D and every shape in Pile 2 is flat. A good rule must describe what makes BOTH groups different.

questions.question: I have 7 shapes: 3 circles, 2 squares, 1 triangle, and 1 oval. I sort by corners. How many go in the 'has corners' group, and what is the rule?
options: 3 shapes. Rule: corners vs no corners.
4 shapes. Rule: one group has corners.
questions.explain: 2 squares + 1 triangle = 3 shapes with corners. The rule must describe both groups. All these shapes are flat, so 3D is not the right attribute.

questions.question: Riya sorted her shapes. Group 1: circle, oval, and square. Group 2: triangle and rectangle. Riya says: 'Group 1 has no corners. Group 2 has corners.' What went wrong?
options: The rule should be about size, not corners.
The rule names only one group, not both.
A square has corners, so the rule fails.
The rule should be about 3D, not corners.
questions.explain: The rule says Group 1 has no corners, but the square DOES have corners. So the rule does not match the groups. A correct rule must fit every shape in each group.

questions.question: Tom has 4 shapes: a circle, a triangle, a square, and an oval. He wants two groups of 2 by one attribute. What rule works?
options: One group has 3 sides, the other has 4.
The corner group has two shapes in it.
One group is 3D and the other is flat.
One group has corners, one does not.
questions.explain: Circle and oval have no corners. Triangle and square have corners. That makes two equal groups of 2. All four shapes are flat, so 3D vs flat does not work here.

questions.question: Mia puts the big blocks in one bin and the small blocks in another bin. What is Mia's rule?
questions.explain: Look at both bins: one holds big blocks, one holds small blocks, so the rule is size. A rule names the attribute, not just one bin.

questions.question: Ava puts her round buttons in a cup. She puts her square buttons in a box. What is Ava's rule?
questions.explain: Round went in the cup and square went in the box, so she sorted by shape. Telling only about the cup misses half the rule.

questions.question: Ben's ball and can roll away. His cube and box will not roll. What rule did Ben use?
questions.explain: The things that roll went one way and the things that stay put went the other way, so the rule is rolling. Colour and size do not split these groups.

questions.question: Ken sorted his beads and said 'This pile is all the red ones.' He did not tell the whole rule. What should Ken say?
questions.explain: One pile is red, so the other pile is a different colour, and the rule is colour. A sorting rule must tell about both piles.

questions.question: On a walk, Eli puts the smooth rocks in one pocket. He puts the bumpy rocks in the other pocket. What is Eli's rule?
options: Sorted by how big they are
questions.explain: Smooth in one pocket and bumpy in the other means he sorted by how they feel. Saying only smooth leaves out the bumpy pocket.

questions.question: Jun has 2 circles and 2 triangles. They are all red and all the same size. Which rule can sort them into two groups?
questions.explain: Every shape is red and the same size, so those cannot split them. Corners can: triangles have corners and circles have none.

questions.question: Kai has 5 star stickers, all the same size. 2 are shiny and 3 are plain. Which rule sorts them into two groups?
options: Sort by how big they are
questions.explain: All 5 are stars of the same size, so shiny or plain is the only attribute that makes two groups. Naming just the shiny ones is only half a rule.

questions.question: Nash lines up the water bottles after soccer. Tall bottles go in one row and short bottles go in another row. What is his rule?
questions.explain: Tall in one row and short in the other means the rule is height. Naming just the tall row tells about one group only.

questions.question: Zoe put 3 big blocks in one pile and 2 small blocks in the other pile. Both piles have red and blue blocks, and Zoe says 'I sorted by colour.' What went wrong?
options: She sorted by size, not colour
She only named the small pile
She sorted by shape, not colour
She sorted by corners, not colour
questions.explain: Both piles hold red and blue, so colour cannot be the rule. The piles really split by size: big in one, small in the other.

questions.question: Tess sorts 9 shapes into two hoops by corners. 5 of the shapes have corners. What is the rule for both hoops, and how many shapes are in the other hoop?
questions.explain: 9 take away 5 leaves 4 shapes with no corners. The rule has to name both hoops: has corners and has no corners.

questions.question: Nia has a triangle, a square, a rectangle, and one more triangle. She makes two groups of 2. What is Nia's rule?
options: Sorted by how big they are
questions.explain: The two triangles have 3 sides and the square and rectangle have 4 sides, so she sorted by number of sides. Counting sides tells you where each shape goes.

questions.question: Jonah says 'My pile is the pointy ones.' Aria says 'I sorted by corners.' Who told the sorting rule?
options: Jonah, he named his pointy pile
Both, pointy and colour are fine
Jonah, he sorted by their size
questions.explain: Aria named an attribute, corners, so her rule tells about both groups. Saying 'the pointy ones' describes one pile only.
